A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

A bounded $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann
integrable if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some grid $P$ satisfies
$U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

derivations.claim: For a positive integer $n$, partition each coordinate into $[k/n,(k+1)/n]$, $0\le k<n$, and write $C_k$ for the product cell with lower vertex $\ell_k=(k_1/n,\ldots,k_d/n)$ and upper vertex $u_k=((k_1+1)/n,\ldots,(k_d+1)/n)$. Coordinatewise monotonicity gives $\inf_{C_k}h=h(\ell_k)$ and $\sup_{C_k}h=h(u_k)$. Each cell volume is $n^{-d}$, so its contribution to $U-L$ is $n^{-d}(h(u_k)-h(\ell_k))$.

For each $k$, let $z_k^{(j)}$ have its first $j$ coordinates at the upper knots of $C_k$ and the remaining coordinates at the lower knots, for $0\le j\le d$. Then $z_k^{(0)}=\ell_k$, $z_k^{(d)}=u_k$, and $h(u_k)-h(\ell_k)=\sum_{j=1}^d(h(z_k^{(j)})-h(z_k^{(j-1)}))$; all summands are nonnegative. Fix $j$ and the other $d-1$ indices. Summing its increments over $k_j=0,\ldots,n-1$ telescopes to $h(y_1)-h(y_0)$, where $y_0,y_1$ have the other coordinates at the selected lower or upper knots and the $j$th coordinates $0,1$. Since $\mathbf0\le y_0\le y_1\le\mathbf1$, this is at most $h(\mathbf1)-h(\mathbf0)$. There are $n^{d-1}$ choices of the other indices for each $j$, so $\sum_k(h(u_k)-h(\ell_k))\le d n^{d-1}(h(\mathbf1)-h(\mathbf0))$.

By step 1.1, the grid's Darboux gap is at most $d(h(\mathbf1)-h(\mathbf0))/n$. Choose $n$ large enough using [F4] to make this less than any prescribed positive tolerance (if the range is zero, every gap is zero). The criterion [F3] then gives Riemann integrability.

Fix $d\ge1$ and a real function $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$. For each nonempty coordinate subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, restrict $f$ to the face adjacent to the all-ones corner by setting
$$f_u(x_u):=f(z),\qquad z_j=\begin{cases}x_j,&j\in u,\\1,&j\notin u.\end{cases}$$
For a finite coordinate grid on $[0,1]^{|u|}$, write its cells as $R_k=\prod_{j\in u}[t_{j,k_j},t_{j,k_j+1}]$. For a cell with lower and upper vertices $a,b$, define its alternating increment
$$\Delta(f_u;R_k):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{|u|}}(-1)^{|u|-|\epsilon|}f_u(z_\epsilon),$$
where $(z_\epsilon)_j=a_j$ if $\epsilon_j=0$ and $(z_\epsilon)_j=b_j$ if $\epsilon_j=1$. The **Vitali variation** of $f_u$ is
$$V_V(f_u):=\sup_{\text{finite coordinate grids on }[0,1]^{|u|}}\ \sum_k|\Delta(f_u;R_k)|.$$
The **Hardy–Krause variation anchored at the upper corner** is
$$V_{HK,1}(f):=\sum_{\emptyset\ne u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}V_V(f_u),$$
with value $+infty$ if any summand is infinite. For $d=1$ this is the ordinary total variation on $[0,1]$. The anchor is part of the convention: every coordinate outside $u$ is fixed at $1$. The smooth mixed-derivative formula for this convention is proved separately for $C^d$ functions.

The same Vitali-variation definition applies on a nondegenerate rectangle
$R=\prod_{j=1}^q[a_j,b_j]$: each coordinate grid starts at $a_j$ and ends at
$b_j$. For a subrectangle $R\subseteq[0,1]^d$, write $V_{HK,1}(f;R)$ for the
sum of the Vitali variations of its face restrictions with complementary
coordinates fixed at the upper endpoints of $R$. If a varied side has length
zero, that face's Vitali variation is defined to be zero. For $R=[0,1]^d$ this
notation is exactly $V_{HK,1}(f)$.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous ([[def-metric-continuity]]). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
([[def-metric-uniform-continuity]]).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
([[thm-lebesgue-number-lemma]]).

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$, with the norms
of [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]. Then:

1. $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]).
2. For $n \ge 1$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.
3. **The dictionary.** For $n \ge 1$ and all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert x-y\rVert_1 = d_1(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_2 = d_2(x,y), \qquad \lVert x-y\rVert_\infty = d_\infty(x,y),$$
   where $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are the metrics of the published
   [[lem-metrics-on-rn]]. So the metric induced by each of these three norms
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]) **is** the correspondingly named published
   metric, not merely one equivalent to it.

**Consequence, used repeatedly below and stated once here.** By clause 3 at
$p = 2$, the metric space $(\mathbb{R}^{n}, d_2)$ of the published metric-spaces
page and the metric space underlying the normed space
$(\mathbb{R}^{n}, \lVert\cdot\rVert_2)$ of this page are the same object. Hence
completeness ([[thm-euclidean-space-complete]] clause 2), Heine-Borel
([[thm-heine-borel-rn]] clause 2) and the compactness equivalences
([[thm-metric-compactness-equivalences]]) are statements about this page's normed
space, **with their hypothesis $n \ge 1$ inherited unchanged and not weakened**.
Nothing below cites any of those three theorems for $n = 0$.

**Why this lemma exists.** Without it the library would hold a norm-induced
metric on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and a separately published metric on the same set with
no recorded relation, and every later citation would have to guess which was
meant. The proof of clause 3 is a comparison of two written expressions; the
value is that the comparison is made and recorded.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

Let $A\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ and $B\subseteq\mathbb R^q$ be nondegenerate closed rectangles, and let $f:A\times B\to\mathbb R$ be Riemann integrable. Then the four lower and upper section-integral functions of [[def-sections-and-iterated-riemann-integrals]] are Riemann integrable and
$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

If the $B$-sections are integrable outside a content-zero set $N\subseteq A$, every bounded exceptionally completed function $h$ with $h(x)=\int_Bf_x$ for $x\notin N$ is integrable and
$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$
The same assertion holds with the coordinate blocks exchanged. In particular, when every section in an order is integrable, the ordinary iterated integral in that order exists and equals the multiple integral. The theorem does not assert that every section of an integrable function is integrable.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

A bounded function on a nondegenerate rectangle is Darboux integrable with
value $I$ if and only if all tagged grid sums converge with mesh to $I$.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

The relation of [[def-real-order]] is well defined and makes $\mathbb{R}$
([[thm-reals-field]]) a totally ordered field.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and let $x, y \in F$. Then

$$\bigl| |x| - |y| \bigr| \le |x - y|.$$

derivations.claim: Fix a nonempty $u=\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}$ and a product cell $R=\prod_{j\in u}[a_j,b_j]$ in a finite coordinate grid of its face. Put $g=f_u$ and $h=\partial_{j_q}\cdots\partial_{j_1}g$, using the continuous derivative extension. Apply [F2] successively in coordinates $j_1,\ldots,j_q$. If a line lies on the boundary because some other coordinates are fixed at $0$ or $1$, approximate those fixed coordinates by interior values and pass to the limit: every intermediate mixed partial and its derivative have continuous extensions, hence are uniformly continuous by [F3]. The integrands therefore converge uniformly along the line, so the integral difference is bounded by the interval length times a uniform error tending to zero; endpoint values converge as well. At each application the finite alternating differences in the remaining coordinates commute with the integral, yielding exactly the alternating sum over the $2^q$ vertices. By [F4] and [F5] this iterated integral equals the product-rectangle Riemann integral, so $\Delta(g;R)=\int_Rh$. Consequently $|\Delta(g;R)|\le\int_R|h|$. Summing over cells and using the absolute-value estimate and finite grid-cell additivity from [F6] gives $\sum_R|\Delta(g;R)|\le\int_{[0,1]^q}|h|$. Taking the supremum over grids proves $V_V(g)\le\int|h|$.

Conversely, fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F3], choose $\delta_1>0$ so that $|h(x)-h(y)|<\varepsilon/2$ whenever $d_2(x,y)<\delta_1$. By [F7] applied to the continuous, hence integrable, function $|h|$ ([F4]), choose $\delta_2>0$ so every tagged grid of mesh below $\delta_2$ has sum within $\varepsilon/2$ of $\int|h|$. By [F8], choose $n$ with $\eta=1/n<\min\{\delta_1/(q+1),\delta_2\}$ and take the uniform product grid of side width $\eta$. For any two points in one cell, each coordinate difference is at most $\eta$, so [F3] gives $d_2(x,y)^2\le q\eta^2<\delta_1^2$ because $q<(q+1)^2$; hence $d_2(x,y)<\delta_1$. Tag each cell at its lower corner $\xi_R$. By [F6], linearity and the constant-integral formula give $\int_Rh=h(\xi_R)\operatorname{vol}(R)+\int_R(h-h(\xi_R))$. Since $|h(x)-h(\xi_R)|<\varepsilon/2$ throughout $R$, monotonicity and the absolute-value estimate in [F6] give $\left|\int_R(h-h(\xi_R))\right|\le\int_R|h-h(\xi_R)|\le(\varepsilon/2)\operatorname{vol}(R)$. Applying [F9] to $a=h(\xi_R)\operatorname{vol}(R)$ and $b=\int_R(h-h(\xi_R))$ yields $|\int_Rh|\ge|h(\xi_R)|\operatorname{vol}(R)-(\varepsilon/2)\operatorname{vol}(R)$. Summing, using that cell volumes total $1$, and applying [F7] to the chosen tags gives $\sum_R|\int_Rh|\ge\sum_R|h(\xi_R)|\operatorname{vol}(R)-\varepsilon/2\ge\int|h|-\varepsilon$. The variation supremum is at least this sum, and arbitrary $\varepsilon$ gives $V_V(g)\ge\int|h|$.
Thus $V_V(f_u)=\int|\partial_u f(x_u;1_{-u})|$ for each nonempty $u$. Summing these finitely many equalities and using [F1] gives the displayed formula.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$. A point multiset is a finite ordered list $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ with $N\ge1$ and $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{id})\in[0,1)^d$; repeated points are counted with their multiplicities. For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in[0,1]^d$, its anchored half-open box and its volume are
$$B(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j),\qquad \operatorname{vol}(B(u)):=\prod_{j=1}^d u_j.$$
The **star discrepancy** of $P$ is
$$D_N^*(P):=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^d}\left|\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mathbf 1_{B(u)}(x_i)-\prod_{j=1}^d u_j\right|.$$
An infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is **uniformly distributed** if $D_N^*(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
For a bounded Riemann-integrable $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$, the **cube integral** and the point-set **cube quadrature** are
$$I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad Q_P(f):=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}f(x_i),$$
where $I_d$ is the Riemann integral of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]. No randomness is part of $Q_P$.

Let $b\ge2$ be an integer. A **base-$b$ elementary interval** in dimension $d$ is
$$E=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_jb^{-k_j},(a_j+1)b^{-k_j}),$$
where each $k_j\ge0$ and each $a_j$ is an integer with $0\le a_j<b^{k_j}$. For integers $m\ge0$ and $0\le t\le m$, a point multiset $P$ is a **$(t,m,d)$-net in base $b$** if it has $b^m$ entries and every base-$b$ elementary interval with $\sum_{j=1}^d k_j=m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ entries, counted with multiplicity. Fix $d\ge1$ and a real function $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$. For each nonempty coordinate subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, restrict $f$ to the face adjacent to the all-ones corner by setting
$$f_u(x_u):=f(z),\qquad z_j=\begin{cases}x_j,&j\in u,\\1,&j\notin u.\end{cases}$$
For a finite coordinate grid on $[0,1]^{|u|}$, write its cells as $R_k=\prod_{j\in u}[t_{j,k_j},t_{j,k_j+1}]$. For a cell with lower and upper vertices $a,b$, define its alternating increment
$$\Delta(f_u;R_k):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{|u|}}(-1)^{|u|-|\epsilon|}f_u(z_\epsilon),$$
where $(z_\epsilon)_j=a_j$ if $\epsilon_j=0$ and $(z_\epsilon)_j=b_j$ if $\epsilon_j=1$. The **Vitali variation** of $f_u$ is
$$V_V(f_u):=\sup_{\text{finite coordinate grids on }[0,1]^{|u|}}\ \sum_k|\Delta(f_u;R_k)|.$$
The **Hardy–Krause variation anchored at the upper corner** is
$$V_{HK,1}(f):=\sum_{\emptyset\ne u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}V_V(f_u),$$
with value $+infty$ if any summand is infinite. For $d=1$ this is the ordinary total variation on $[0,1]$. The anchor is part of the convention: every coordinate outside $u$ is fixed at $1$. The smooth mixed-derivative formula for this convention is proved separately for $C^d$ functions.

The same Vitali-variation definition applies on a nondegenerate rectangle
$R=\prod_{j=1}^q[a_j,b_j]$: each coordinate grid starts at $a_j$ and ends at
$b_j$. For a subrectangle $R\subseteq[0,1]^d$, write $V_{HK,1}(f;R)$ for the
sum of the Vitali variations of its face restrictions with complementary
coordinates fixed at the upper endpoints of $R$. If a varied side has length
zero, that face's Vitali variation is defined to be zero. For $R=[0,1]^d$ this
notation is exactly $V_{HK,1}(f)$.

Let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ and let $R=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_j,b_j]\subseteq[0,1]^d$
be a closed axis-parallel rectangle, allowing zero side lengths. For each
nonempty subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, define the lower-face restriction
$$f_{u,0,R}(x_u):=f(z),\qquad z_j=\begin{cases}x_j,&j\in u,\\a_j,&j\notin u.\end{cases}$$
If every side indexed by $u$ is nondegenerate, its Vitali variation on
$\prod_{j\in u}[a_j,b_j]$ is the supremum of the sums of absolute alternating
increments over finite product grids on that rectangle, using the convention
of [[def-hardykrause-variation]]. If any side indexed by $u$ has length zero,
that term is defined to be zero. The **Hardy–Krause variation on $R$ anchored
at its lower corner** is
$$V_{HK,0}(f;R):=\sum_{\emptyset\ne u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}V_V(f_{u,0,R};\prod_{j\in u}[a_j,b_j]),$$
with value $+\infty$ if any summand is infinite. Write
$V_{HK,0}(f):=V_{HK,0}(f;[0,1]^d)$. The lower anchor fixes every complementary
coordinate at the lower endpoint of $R$; this auxiliary convention is distinct
from the upper anchor used in [[def-hardykrause-variation]].

Let $d\ge1$ and let $h:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ be bounded and nondecreasing in
each coordinate while the other coordinates are fixed. Then $h$ is Riemann
integrable on $[0,1]^d$.

Let $Q=\prod_{j<m}[a_j,b_j]$ be nondegenerate. For integrable
$f,g:Q\to\mathbb R$ and scalars $\alpha,\beta$, the function
$\alpha f+\beta g$ is integrable and its integral is
$\alpha\int_Qf+\beta\int_Qg$. If $f\le g$, then
$\int_Qf\le\int_Qg$. Also $|f|$ is integrable and
$|\int_Qf|\le\int_Q|f|$. If $a_r<c<b_r$, cutting $Q$ at the coordinate
hyperplane $x_r=c$ gives two nondegenerate subrectangles; integrability on
$Q$ is equivalent to integrability on both restrictions, and their integral
values add to the integral over $Q$.

A bounded $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle is Riemann
integrable if and only if, for every $\varepsilon>0$, some grid $P$ satisfies
$U(f,P)-L(f,P)<\varepsilon$.

derivations.claim: Let $\rho(x)=\mathbf1-x$ and $g=f\circ\rho$. Reflection sends each upper face of $f$ to the corresponding lower face of $g$, sends each product grid to a product grid, and reverses the sign of an alternating increment by at most a factor $(-1)^{|u|}$. Its absolute value is unchanged. Hence $V_{HK,0}(g)=V_{HK,1}(f)<\infty$.

For $x\in[0,1]^d$, put $v(x)=V_{HK,0}(g;[0,x])$. Every grid on a smaller face rectangle extends to a grid on the corresponding whole face by inserting the smaller rectangle's upper endpoints as knots; the old cells remain and the added absolute-increment terms are nonnegative. Hence each face variation on $[0,x]$ is at most the corresponding whole-face variation, and enlarging an upper endpoint cannot decrease it. Thus $0\le v(x)\le V_{HK,0}(g)$ and $v$ is nondecreasing in each coordinate.

Fix a coordinate $j$, fix the other coordinates $x_{-j}$, and let $0\le a<b\le1$. Write $x^a,x^b$ for the vectors with $j$th coordinate $a,b$. Terms in $v$ whose varied-coordinate set omits $j$ cancel in $v(x^b)-v(x^a)$. For a term whose set is $A\cup\{j\}$, additivity of Vitali variation at the split $[0,a]\cup[a,b]$ shows that its difference is the Vitali variation on the face rectangle $R_A$ with $j$ interval $[a,b]$, coordinates in $A$ intervals $[0,x_i]$, and all remaining coordinates fixed at $0$. Additivity follows directly by inserting $a$ into every grid: refinement and the triangle inequality give one inequality, while joining grids whose sums approach the two suprema gives the reverse inequality. Therefore $v(x^b)-v(x^a)=\sum_{A\subseteq[d]\setminus\{j\}}V_V(g_{A\cup\{j\},0};R_A)$.

Expanding the right side of the finite-difference identity by inclusion–exclusion gives $g(x^b)-g(x^a)=\sum_{A\subseteq[d]\setminus\{j\}}\Delta_{A\cup\{j\}}g(R_A)$: every vertex with a coordinate outside $A\cup\{j\}$ set to $0$ cancels with the same vertex from the term with that coordinate added to $A$, leaving only the two vertices with all other coordinates equal to $x_{-j}$. Each one-cell grid shows $V_V(g_{A\cup\{j\},0};R_A)\ge|\Delta_{A\cup\{j\}}g(R_A)|$. The triangle inequality and step 3.1 now give $v(x^b)-v(x^a)\ge|g(x^b)-g(x^a)|$. Consequently both $v$ and $w:=v-g$ are nondecreasing in every coordinate.

The function $v$ is bounded by step 2.1. The function $w$ is finite-valued and coordinatewise nondecreasing, so $w(\mathbf0)\le w(x)\le w(\mathbf1)$ for every $x$ and is bounded as well. By [F3], $v$ and $w$ are Riemann integrable; since $g=v-w$, [F4] makes $g$ Riemann integrable. Reflection preserves boundedness and maps each grid cell to a cell of the same volume with the same infimum and supremum values for $f=g\circ\rho$, so f has the same arbitrarily small Darboux gaps as g. The criterion [F5] makes $f$ Riemann integrable.

Let $N\ge1$, let $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ be a point multiset in $[0,1)^d$, and let $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ have finite upper-anchor Hardy–Krause variation. This finiteness implies that $f$ is bounded and Riemann integrable by [[lem-finite-hardykrause-variation-implies-riemann-integrability]], so $Q_P(f)$ is defined. Let $G$ be a finite coordinate grid containing every coordinate of every point of $P$, with knots $0=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,m_j}=1$. Its lower-corner Riemann sum is
$$C_k:=\prod_{j=1}^d[t_{j,k_j},t_{j,k_j+1}],\qquad S_G(f):=\sum_{0\le k_j<m_j} f(t_{1,k_1},\ldots,t_{d,k_d})\operatorname{vol}(C_k),$$
where the cells and volume convention are those of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]] and [[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]], and $S_G$ is the lower-corner tagged Riemann sum of [[def-multidimensional-tagged-partition-and-riemann-sum]].
Then $\left|Q_P(f)-S_G(f)\right|\le D_N^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f)$, with the quadrature and star discrepancy of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]] and the variation of [[def-hardykrause-variation]].

A bounded function on a nondegenerate rectangle is Darboux integrable with
value $I$ if and only if all tagged grid sums converge with mesh to $I$.

A **grid partition** $P$ of a nondegenerate rectangle $Q=[a,b]\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ is a family, one for each $j<m$, of one-dimensional partitions $a_j=t_{j,0}<\cdots<t_{j,n_j}=b_j$ ([[def-partition-and-refinement]]). For a multi-index $i=(i_0,\ldots,i_{m-1})$ with $i_j<n_j$, its cell is
$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) and let
$\varepsilon \in F$ with $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there is a natural number
$n \ge 1$ such that

$$\frac{1}{n \cdot 1_F} < \varepsilon ,$$

where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of $F$ ([[thm-of-archimedean]]) and
$1/(n \cdot 1_F)$ is its multiplicative inverse ([[def-field]]). As is standard
we abbreviate $n \cdot 1_F$ to $n$ and write the conclusion $1/n < \varepsilon$.

This is the **reciprocal form** of the Archimedean property.
[[thm-of-archimedean]] on its own delivers only the assertion that the canonical
naturals are cofinal, $x < n \cdot 1_F$; the form actually used in analysis, that
the reciprocals of the naturals get below every positive bound, is the statement
above, and it is recorded separately so that no proof has to reconstruct the
inversion step in passing.

Hardy–Krause variation $V_{HK,1}(f)$ as defined in
[[def-hardykrause-variation]]. Then $f$ is bounded and Riemann integrable on
$[0,1]^d$.

Applying [F1] to each $G_r$ gives $|Q_P(f)-S_{G_r}(f)|\le D_N^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f)$ for every $r$.

By [F4], $f$ is bounded and Riemann integrable. The mesh of $G_r$ tends to zero, so [F2] gives $S_{G_r}(f)\to I_d(f)$. Since $Q_P(f)$ and the bound on the right are fixed, continuity of absolute value passes the inequality in step 2.1 to the limit and yields the stated Koksma–Hlawka bound.

**Inputs:** a dimension $d\ge1$, a function $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ that is finite at each generated node, and exactly one of the following point-set specifications:

1. **Digital branch:** a prime $p$, an integer $m\ge1$, and matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$. Optionally supply an integer $t$ with $0\le t\le m$ when the caller also wants the exact $(t,m,d)$-net property checked.
2. **General lattice-rule branch:** a full-rank discrete additive subgroup $L\subset\mathbb R^d$ containing $\mathbb Z^d$, with finite quotient $L/\mathbb Z^d$, and a supplied complete list $P$ of the distinct coset representatives in $[0,1)^d$.
3. **Rank-one lattice branch:** an integer $N\ge1$ and $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $\gcd(z_1,N)=1$, where $\gcd$ has the convention of [[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]].

**Outputs:** The ordered point list $P$, the finite node average $A_P(f)$, and, when $t$ is supplied in the digital branch, the net-count check result.

A lattice rule means the equal-weight rule on the representatives of an integration lattice $L$ as in branch 2; its node count is $N=|L/\mathbb Z^d|$. Branch 3 specifies the rank-one fractional-part construction.

**Instructions:**

1. In the digital branch, for each $n=0,\ldots,p^m-1$, write $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$, form $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Replace each coordinate $y^{(j)}_r$ by its representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ and set $x_{n,j}=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}$. The output point list is $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^m-1})$. If $t$ was supplied, enumerate every integer tuple $k_1,\ldots,k_d\ge0$ with $\sum_jk_j=m-t$ and every tuple $a_j\in\{0,\ldots,p^{k_j}-1\}$; count the output nodes in each corresponding elementary interval. Return “net check passed” exactly when every count equals $p^t$, and otherwise return “not a $(t,m,d)$-net.”
2. In the general lattice-rule branch, take the supplied complete list $P$ of representatives; do not add further points or repeat any coset representative.
3. In the rank-one lattice branch, for each $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, set $x_{n,j}=\{nz_j/N\}$ for $j=1,\ldots,d$, where $\{a\}:=a-\lfloor a\rfloor\in[0,1)$ and $\lfloor a\rfloor$ is the integer part from [[lem-integer-part]]. The output point list is $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$.
4. In each branch, let $N$ be the output list length and return the finite node average $A_P(f):=N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(x_n)$ together with $P$. In the digital branch $N=p^m$; in the general lattice branch $N=|L/\mathbb Z^d|$. When $f$ is bounded and Riemann integrable, $A_P(f)=Q_P(f)$ and its target is the cube integral $I_d(f)$ of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]]. For other admissible inputs the finite average is still defined, but no cube-integral target is asserted. The algorithm does not estimate a discrepancy, a variation, or a sampling variance, and a generated digital point set has no claimed net quality unless the optional count check passes.

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$. A point multiset is a finite ordered list $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ with $N\ge1$ and $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{id})\in[0,1)^d$; repeated points are counted with their multiplicities. For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in[0,1]^d$, its anchored half-open box and its volume are
$$B(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j),\qquad \operatorname{vol}(B(u)):=\prod_{j=1}^d u_j.$$
The **star discrepancy** of $P$ is
$$D_N^*(P):=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^d}\left|\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mathbf 1_{B(u)}(x_i)-\prod_{j=1}^d u_j\right|.$$
An infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is **uniformly distributed** if $D_N^*(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
For a bounded Riemann-integrable $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$, the **cube integral** and the point-set **cube quadrature** are
$$I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad Q_P(f):=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}f(x_i),$$
where $I_d$ is the Riemann integral of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]. No randomness is part of $Q_P$.

Let $b\ge2$ be an integer. A **base-$b$ elementary interval** in dimension $d$ is
$$E=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_jb^{-k_j},(a_j+1)b^{-k_j}),$$
where each $k_j\ge0$ and each $a_j$ is an integer with $0\le a_j<b^{k_j}$. For integers $m\ge0$ and $0\le t\le m$, a point multiset $P$ is a **$(t,m,d)$-net in base $b$** if it has $b^m$ entries and every base-$b$ elementary interval with $\sum_{j=1}^d k_j=m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ entries, counted with multiplicity. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is a **$(t,d)$-sequence in base $b$** if for every $m\ge t$ and $k\ge0$, the aligned block $(x_{kb^m},\ldots,x_{(k+1)b^m-1})$ is a $(t,m,d)$-net.

For a prime integer $p$, we have $p\ge2$ ([[def-prime]]). Write $\mathbb F_p:=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, which is a field by [[thm-z-mod-p-is-a-field]]. By [[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], each residue class has exactly one representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, and every $n\in\{0,\ldots,p^m-1\}$ has a unique base-$p$ expansion $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$ with digits $n_{r-1}\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$. The integer powers use [[def-integer-power]]. A **digital point set** in base $p$ is generated from matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$ as follows. For each such $n$, let $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, interpreting each digit as its residue class, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Taking the unique representatives $y^{(j)}_r\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, set
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}.$$
Since $0\le y^{(j)}_r\le p-1$, the finite geometric sum gives $0\le x_{n,j}\le\sum_{r=1}^m(p-1)p^{-r}=1-p^{-m}<1$; the identity follows by telescoping with the integer-power laws [[lem-power-laws]], and $p^{-m}>0$ by [[lem-power-monotone]] and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]. It is a **digital $(t,m,d)$-net** only if this generated point multiset also satisfies the stated $(t,m,d)$-net counting condition; arbitrary generator matrices need not do so.

A **digital sequence** is generated by infinite matrices $C_j=(c^{(j)}_{r,k})_{r,k\ge1}$ over $\mathbb F_p$. For each $n\ge0$, pad its finite base-$p$ expansion with zero digits and, for every $r,j$, compute the finite field sum $y_{r,j}(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{(j)}_{r,k}n_{k-1}$; only finitely many summands are nonzero. Let $\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ be its unique integer representative. The output coordinate is the real series
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}.$$
This series is defined by [[def-series]] and converges: its terms satisfy $0\le\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}\le(p-1)p^{-r}$; since $p\ge2$, [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $p^{-1}\in(0,1)$, and the bounding geometric series $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(p-1)p^{-r}$ converges to $1$ by [[thm-geometric-series]]. The comparison theorem [[thm-direct-comparison-test]] therefore gives convergence of the output series. Its sum lies in $[0,1]$; the resulting points are required to lie in $[0,1)^d$. It is a digital $(t,d)$-sequence when it also satisfies the aligned-block net condition above. No discrepancy rate follows from these definitions alone.

Let $a, d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \mid a$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]) and $a \ne 0$.
Then $d \ne 0$ and

$$|d| \;\le\; |a| .$$

Consequently, for $a \ne 0$ the set $\{\, d \in \mathbb{Z} : d \mid a \,\}$ of
divisors of $a$ is bounded above by $|a|$: every divisor $d$ of $a$ satisfies
$d \le |a|$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$. An integer $d$ is a **common divisor** of $a$ and $b$
when $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]). Write

$$D(a,b) \;:=\; \{\, d \in \mathbb{Z} \;:\; d \mid a \ \text{ and } \ d \mid b \,\}$$

for the set of common divisors.

**Case $(a,b) \ne (0,0)$: the greatest element exists.** $D(a,b)$ is nonempty,
since $1 \mid a$ and $1 \mid b$ for every $a$ and $b$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]). It
is bounded above: at least one of $a$ and $b$ is nonzero, say $a \ne 0$ (if
instead $b \ne 0$, argue with $b$ throughout), and every $d \in D(a,b)$ divides
$a$, so $d \le |a|$ by [[lem-divisor-bound]]. A nonempty set of integers bounded
above has a unique greatest element ([[lem-int-bounded-above-has-greatest]]), and
we define

$$\gcd(a,b) \;:=\; \text{the greatest element of } D(a,b).$$

Since $1 \in D(a,b)$ and $\gcd(a,b)$ is greatest, $\gcd(a,b) \ge 1$; in
particular $\gcd(a,b) > 0$.

**Case $(a,b) = (0,0)$: a convention, fixed here.** Every integer divides $0$
([[def-divides-in-z]]), so $D(0,0) = \mathbb{Z}$, which has no greatest element
at all: the clause above defines nothing, and leaving $\gcd(0,0)$ undefined would
put a hole in every identity below. We therefore set

$$\gcd(0,0) \;:=\; 0 .$$

With both cases together, $\gcd(a,b)$ is defined for every pair of integers, and
$\gcd(a,b) \ge 0$ always.

**Why $0$, and not some other value.** The convention is not arbitrary, and the
reasons are recorded here rather than deferred:

- **It is the greatest common divisor in the divisibility ordering.** $0$ is a
  common divisor of $0$ and $0$, and every common divisor of $0$ and $0$ divides
  $0$. So $0$ is greatest at $(0,0)$ in the sense "divisible by every common
  divisor", which is the sense that [[cor-common-divisor-divides-gcd]] shows
  holds at **every** pair, $(0,0)$ included, whereas "greatest in the order of
  $\mathbb{Z}$" fails there.
- **It is the only value under which the scaling identity extends to this
  boundary.** Requiring $\gcd(ca,cb) = |c|\gcd(a,b)$ to hold at every triple
  leaves no freedom here. At $c = 0$ with any $(a,b) \ne (0,0)$ it would read
  $\gcd(0,0) = |0|\gcd(a,b) = 0$, whose right-hand side does not involve
  $\gcd(0,0)$ at all; and at $a = b = 0$ with $c = 1 + 1$ it reads $g = g + g$,
  again giving $g = 0$. The value is therefore chosen here, and
  [[lem-gcd-scaling]] then proves the identity for every triple with this
  convention in force; its own $(0,0)$ case reads the value off this definition
  rather than establishing it.
- **It is consistent with the product formula** —
  $\gcd(a,b)\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = |ab|$ ([[thm-gcd-lcm-product]]) reads
  $0 \cdot 0 = 0$ at $(0,0)$, using $\operatorname{lcm}(0,0) = 0$ from

Fix an integer dimension $d\ge1$. A point multiset is a finite ordered list $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ with $N\ge1$ and $x_i=(x_{i1},\ldots,x_{id})\in[0,1)^d$; repeated points are counted with their multiplicities. For $u=(u_1,\ldots,u_d)\in[0,1]^d$, its anchored half-open box and its volume are
$$B(u):=\prod_{j=1}^d[0,u_j),\qquad \operatorname{vol}(B(u)):=\prod_{j=1}^d u_j.$$
The **star discrepancy** of $P$ is
$$D_N^*(P):=\sup_{u\in[0,1]^d}\left|\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}\mathbf 1_{B(u)}(x_i)-\prod_{j=1}^d u_j\right|.$$
An infinite sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is **uniformly distributed** if $D_N^*(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
For a bounded Riemann-integrable $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$, the **cube integral** and the point-set **cube quadrature** are
$$I_d(f):=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(x)\,dx,\qquad Q_P(f):=\frac1N\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}f(x_i),$$
where $I_d$ is the Riemann integral of [[def-multidimensional-darboux-integral]]. No randomness is part of $Q_P$.

Let $b\ge2$ be an integer. A **base-$b$ elementary interval** in dimension $d$ is
$$E=\prod_{j=1}^d[a_jb^{-k_j},(a_j+1)b^{-k_j}),$$
where each $k_j\ge0$ and each $a_j$ is an integer with $0\le a_j<b^{k_j}$. For integers $m\ge0$ and $0\le t\le m$, a point multiset $P$ is a **$(t,m,d)$-net in base $b$** if it has $b^m$ entries and every base-$b$ elementary interval with $\sum_{j=1}^d k_j=m-t$ contains exactly $b^t$ entries, counted with multiplicity. A sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ in $[0,1)^d$ is a **$(t,d)$-sequence in base $b$** if for every $m\ge t$ and $k\ge0$, the aligned block $(x_{kb^m},\ldots,x_{(k+1)b^m-1})$ is a $(t,m,d)$-net.

For a prime integer $p$, we have $p\ge2$ ([[def-prime]]). Write $\mathbb F_p:=\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$, which is a field by [[thm-z-mod-p-is-a-field]]. By [[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], each residue class has exactly one representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, and every $n\in\{0,\ldots,p^m-1\}$ has a unique base-$p$ expansion $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$ with digits $n_{r-1}\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$. The integer powers use [[def-integer-power]]. A **digital point set** in base $p$ is generated from matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$ as follows. For each such $n$, let $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, interpreting each digit as its residue class, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Taking the unique representatives $y^{(j)}_r\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, set
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}.$$
Since $0\le y^{(j)}_r\le p-1$, the finite geometric sum gives $0\le x_{n,j}\le\sum_{r=1}^m(p-1)p^{-r}=1-p^{-m}<1$; the identity follows by telescoping with the integer-power laws [[lem-power-laws]], and $p^{-m}>0$ by [[lem-power-monotone]] and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]. It is a **digital $(t,m,d)$-net** only if this generated point multiset also satisfies the stated $(t,m,d)$-net counting condition; arbitrary generator matrices need not do so.

A **digital sequence** is generated by infinite matrices $C_j=(c^{(j)}_{r,k})_{r,k\ge1}$ over $\mathbb F_p$. For each $n\ge0$, pad its finite base-$p$ expansion with zero digits and, for every $r,j$, compute the finite field sum $y_{r,j}(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{(j)}_{r,k}n_{k-1}$; only finitely many summands are nonzero. Let $\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ be its unique integer representative. The output coordinate is the real series
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}.$$
This series is defined by [[def-series]] and converges: its terms satisfy $0\le\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}\le(p-1)p^{-r}$; since $p\ge2$, [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $p^{-1}\in(0,1)$, and the bounding geometric series $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(p-1)p^{-r}$ converges to $1$ by [[thm-geometric-series]]. The comparison theorem [[thm-direct-comparison-test]] therefore gives convergence of the output series. Its sum lies in $[0,1]$; the resulting points are required to lie in $[0,1)^d$. It is a digital $(t,d)$-sequence when it also satisfies the aligned-block net condition above. No discrepancy rate follows from these definitions alone.

**Inputs:** a dimension $d\ge1$, a function $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ that is finite at each generated node, and exactly one of the following point-set specifications:

1. **Digital branch:** a prime $p$, an integer $m\ge1$, and matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$. Optionally supply an integer $t$ with $0\le t\le m$ when the caller also wants the exact $(t,m,d)$-net property checked.
2. **General lattice-rule branch:** a full-rank discrete additive subgroup $L\subset\mathbb R^d$ containing $\mathbb Z^d$, with finite quotient $L/\mathbb Z^d$, and a supplied complete list $P$ of the distinct coset representatives in $[0,1)^d$.
3. **Rank-one lattice branch:** an integer $N\ge1$ and $z=(z_1,\ldots,z_d)\in\mathbb Z^d$ with $\gcd(z_1,N)=1$, where $\gcd$ has the convention of [[def-common-divisor-and-gcd]].

**Outputs:** The ordered point list $P$, the finite node average $A_P(f)$, and, when $t$ is supplied in the digital branch, the net-count check result.

A lattice rule means the equal-weight rule on the representatives of an integration lattice $L$ as in branch 2; its node count is $N=|L/\mathbb Z^d|$. Branch 3 specifies the rank-one fractional-part construction.

**Instructions:**

1. In the digital branch, for each $n=0,\ldots,p^m-1$, write $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$, form $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Replace each coordinate $y^{(j)}_r$ by its representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ and set $x_{n,j}=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}$. The output point list is $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{p^m-1})$. If $t$ was supplied, enumerate every integer tuple $k_1,\ldots,k_d\ge0$ with $\sum_jk_j=m-t$ and every tuple $a_j\in\{0,\ldots,p^{k_j}-1\}$; count the output nodes in each corresponding elementary interval. Return “net check passed” exactly when every count equals $p^t$, and otherwise return “not a $(t,m,d)$-net.”
2. In the general lattice-rule branch, take the supplied complete list $P$ of representatives; do not add further points or repeat any coset representative.
3. In the rank-one lattice branch, for each $n=0,\ldots,N-1$, set $x_{n,j}=\{nz_j/N\}$ for $j=1,\ldots,d$, where $\{a\}:=a-\lfloor a\rfloor\in[0,1)$ and $\lfloor a\rfloor$ is the integer part from [[lem-integer-part]]. The output point list is $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$.
4. In each branch, let $N$ be the output list length and return the finite node average $A_P(f):=N^{-1}\sum_{n=0}^{N-1}f(x_n)$ together with $P$. In the digital branch $N=p^m$; in the general lattice branch $N=|L/\mathbb Z^d|$. When $f$ is bounded and Riemann integrable, $A_P(f)=Q_P(f)$ and its target is the cube integral $I_d(f)$ of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]]. For other admissible inputs the finite average is still defined, but no cube-integral target is asserted. The algorithm does not estimate a discrepancy, a variation, or a sampling variance, and a generated digital point set has no claimed net quality unless the optional count check passes.

$$\left|Q_P(f)-I_d(f)\right|\le D_N^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f),$$
where $Q_P$, $I_d$, and $D_N^*$ use the conventions of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]], and $V_{HK,1}$ uses the face convention of [[def-hardykrause-variation]]. The point set and integrand are otherwise arbitrary; no construction-specific rate or computability of the two factors is asserted.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

Let $a, d \in \mathbb{Z}$ with $d \mid a$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]) and $a \ne 0$.
Then $d \ne 0$ and

$$|d| \;\le\; |a| .$$

Consequently, for $a \ne 0$ the set $\{\, d \in \mathbb{Z} : d \mid a \,\}$ of
divisors of $a$ is bounded above by $|a|$: every divisor $d$ of $a$ satisfies
$d \le |a|$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{Z}$. An integer $d$ is a **common divisor** of $a$ and $b$
when $d \mid a$ and $d \mid b$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]). Write

$$D(a,b) \;:=\; \{\, d \in \mathbb{Z} \;:\; d \mid a \ \text{ and } \ d \mid b \,\}$$

for the set of common divisors.

**Case $(a,b) \ne (0,0)$: the greatest element exists.** $D(a,b)$ is nonempty,
since $1 \mid a$ and $1 \mid b$ for every $a$ and $b$ ([[def-divides-in-z]]). It
is bounded above: at least one of $a$ and $b$ is nonzero, say $a \ne 0$ (if
instead $b \ne 0$, argue with $b$ throughout), and every $d \in D(a,b)$ divides
$a$, so $d \le |a|$ by [[lem-divisor-bound]]. A nonempty set of integers bounded
above has a unique greatest element ([[lem-int-bounded-above-has-greatest]]), and
we define

$$\gcd(a,b) \;:=\; \text{the greatest element of } D(a,b).$$

Since $1 \in D(a,b)$ and $\gcd(a,b)$ is greatest, $\gcd(a,b) \ge 1$; in
particular $\gcd(a,b) > 0$.

**Case $(a,b) = (0,0)$: a convention, fixed here.** Every integer divides $0$
([[def-divides-in-z]]), so $D(0,0) = \mathbb{Z}$, which has no greatest element
at all: the clause above defines nothing, and leaving $\gcd(0,0)$ undefined would
put a hole in every identity below. We therefore set

$$\gcd(0,0) \;:=\; 0 .$$

With both cases together, $\gcd(a,b)$ is defined for every pair of integers, and
$\gcd(a,b) \ge 0$ always.

**Why $0$, and not some other value.** The convention is not arbitrary, and the
reasons are recorded here rather than deferred:

- **It is the greatest common divisor in the divisibility ordering.** $0$ is a
  common divisor of $0$ and $0$, and every common divisor of $0$ and $0$ divides
  $0$. So $0$ is greatest at $(0,0)$ in the sense "divisible by every common
  divisor", which is the sense that [[cor-common-divisor-divides-gcd]] shows
  holds at **every** pair, $(0,0)$ included, whereas "greatest in the order of
  $\mathbb{Z}$" fails there.
- **It is the only value under which the scaling identity extends to this
  boundary.** Requiring $\gcd(ca,cb) = |c|\gcd(a,b)$ to hold at every triple
  leaves no freedom here. At $c = 0$ with any $(a,b) \ne (0,0)$ it would read
  $\gcd(0,0) = |0|\gcd(a,b) = 0$, whose right-hand side does not involve
  $\gcd(0,0)$ at all; and at $a = b = 0$ with $c = 1 + 1$ it reads $g = g + g$,
  again giving $g = 0$. The value is therefore chosen here, and
  [[lem-gcd-scaling]] then proves the identity for every triple with this
  convention in force; its own $(0,0)$ case reads the value off this definition
  rather than establishing it.
- **It is consistent with the product formula** —
  $\gcd(a,b)\operatorname{lcm}(a,b) = |ab|$ ([[thm-gcd-lcm-product]]) reads
  $0 \cdot 0 = 0$ at $(0,0)$, using $\operatorname{lcm}(0,0) = 0$ from
  [[def-lcm]]. This one is a check, **not** a second forcing argument: with
  $\operatorname{lcm}(0,0) = 0$ the left side vanishes whatever value
  $\gcd(0,0)$ is given, so the product formula is silent at $(0,0)$ and only the
  scaling identity above pins the value down.

This is the $C^d$ hypothesis here, including agreement of the boundary values of $f$ with its order-zero extension. For $u=\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}$, write $\partial_u f$ for the iterated derivative $\partial_{j_q}\cdots\partial_{j_1}f$, interpreted on the closed cube by its continuous extension. For each nonempty $u$, let $f_u(x_u)=f(x_u;1_{-u})$ be the restriction to the face adjacent to the upper corner. Then
$$V_{HK,1}(f)=\sum_{\emptyset\ne u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}\int_{[0,1]^{|u|}}\left|\partial_u f(x_u;1_{-u})\right|\,dx_u,$$
where $V_{HK,1}$ is the upper-anchor variation of [[def-hardykrause-variation]], and $\partial_u$ differentiates once in each coordinate in $u$.

$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

$$Q_i:=\prod_{j<m}[t_{j,i_j},t_{j,i_j+1}].$$
A sum over cells means the iterated recursive sum $\sum_{i_0<n_0}\cdots\sum_{i_{m-1}<n_{m-1}}$ of [[def-finite-sum]]. The **mesh** is $\max_{j<m,i_j<n_j}(t_{j,i_j+1}-t_{j,i_j})$, which exists by [[lem-finite-set-has-max]] and is the largest $d_\infty$-diameter ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]], [[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

Refinement is coordinatewise. Coordinatewise union gives a common refinement. The cells cover $Q$ and have pairwise disjoint interiors. Repeated splitting of finite sums and induction on $m$ give
$$\sum_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i)=\operatorname{vol}(Q).$$
These statements include boundary overlaps: boundaries may meet, but interiors do not, and volume splitting is algebraic.

Let $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ be bounded on a nondegenerate rectangle and let $P$ be a grid. For each cell $Q_i$, put
$$m_i:=\inf f[Q_i],\quad M_i:=\sup f[Q_i],\quad L(f,P):=\sum_i m_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),\quad U(f,P):=\sum_i M_i\operatorname{vol}(Q_i).$$
The extrema exist as finite reals because each nonempty image is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]], [[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]), and the sums use the iterated convention of [[def-multidimensional-grid-partition]].

Since $m_i\le M_i$ and cell volumes are nonnegative, $L(f,P)\le U(f,P)$. Moreover
$$U(f,P)-L(f,P)=\sum_i(M_i-m_i)\operatorname{vol}(Q_i),$$
the sum of cell oscillations weighted by volume ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]).

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle

$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$

degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.
Every continuous real function on a closed nondegenerate rectangle $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $m\ge1$, is Riemann integrable.

$$\int_A\ell_B=\int_Au_B=\int_{A\times B}f=\int_B\ell_A=\int_Bu_A.$$

$$\int_{A\times B}f=\int_Ah.$$

By [[thm-division-algorithm-in-z]], each residue class has exactly one representative in $\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, and every $n\in\{0,\ldots,p^m-1\}$ has a unique base-$p$ expansion $n=\sum_{r=1}^m n_{r-1}p^{r-1}$ with digits $n_{r-1}\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$. The integer powers use [[def-integer-power]]. A **digital point set** in base $p$ is generated from matrices $C_1,\ldots,C_d\in\mathbb F_p^{m\times m}$ as follows. For each such $n$, let $v(n)=(n_0,\ldots,n_{m-1})^T\in\mathbb F_p^m$, interpreting each digit as its residue class, and compute $y^{(j)}=C_jv(n)$ in $\mathbb F_p^m$. Taking the unique representatives $y^{(j)}_r\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$, set
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^m y^{(j)}_r p^{-r}.$$
Since $0\le y^{(j)}_r\le p-1$, the finite geometric sum gives $0\le x_{n,j}\le\sum_{r=1}^m(p-1)p^{-r}=1-p^{-m}<1$; the identity follows by telescoping with the integer-power laws [[lem-power-laws]], and $p^{-m}>0$ by [[lem-power-monotone]] and [[lem-of-inverse-positive]]. It is a **digital $(t,m,d)$-net** only if this generated point multiset also satisfies the stated $(t,m,d)$-net counting condition; arbitrary generator matrices need not do so.

A **digital sequence** is generated by infinite matrices $C_j=(c^{(j)}_{r,k})_{r,k\ge1}$ over $\mathbb F_p$. For each $n\ge0$, pad its finite base-$p$ expansion with zero digits and, for every $r,j$, compute the finite field sum $y_{r,j}(n)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{(j)}_{r,k}n_{k-1}$; only finitely many summands are nonzero. Let $\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)\in\{0,\ldots,p-1\}$ be its unique integer representative. The output coordinate is the real series
$$x_{n,j}:=\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}.$$
This series is defined by [[def-series]] and converges: its terms satisfy $0\le\widetilde y_{r,j}(n)p^{-r}\le(p-1)p^{-r}$; since $p\ge2$, [[lem-of-inverse-positive]] gives $p^{-1}\in(0,1)$, and the bounding geometric series $\sum_{r=1}^{\infty}(p-1)p^{-r}$ converges to $1$ by [[thm-geometric-series]]. The comparison theorem [[thm-direct-comparison-test]] therefore gives convergence of the output series. Its sum lies in $[0,1]$; the resulting points are required to lie in $[0,1)^d$. It is a digital $(t,d)$-sequence when it also satisfies the aligned-block net condition above. No discrepancy rate follows from these definitions alone.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ be a finite nonempty point multiset in $[0,1)^d$. If $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ has finite Hardy–Krause variation anchored at $1$, then
$$\left|Q_P(f)-I_d(f)\right|\le D_N^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f),$$
where $Q_P$, $I_d$, and $D_N^*$ use the conventions of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]], and $V_{HK,1}$ uses the face convention of [[def-hardykrause-variation]]. The point set and integrand are otherwise arbitrary; no construction-specific rate or computability of the two factors is asserted.

derivations.claim: The upper faces are $f(x,1)=x$ and $f(1,y)=y$, and the full mixed derivative is $\partial_{xy}f=1$. By [F1], $V_{HK,1}(f)=\int_0^1 1\,dx+\int_0^1 1\,dy+\int_{[0,1]^2}1\,dx\,dy=1+1+1=3$; the one-dimensional integrals and the square integral of $1$ equal the respective volumes by [F2].

At $u=(1/4,1/2)$ the point is excluded from the half-open anchored box, so the discrepancy there is $1/8$. If $u_1\le1/4$ or $u_2\le1/2$, the box is empty and its volume is at most $1/2$. If both coordinates exceed those thresholds, the box contains the point and its error is $1-u_1u_2\le1-(1/4)(1/2)=7/8$; values approach $7/8$ as $u\downarrow(1/4,1/2)$. Thus $D_1^*(P)=7/8$. Also $Q_P(f)=1/8$. By [F3], the double integral equals the iterated Riemann integral, and [F5] evaluates it as $I_2(f)=\int_0^1 y\left(\int_0^1x\,dx\right)dy=1/4$.
The error is $|1/8-1/4|=1/8\le(7/8)\cdot3=D_1^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f)$, consistent with [F6].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.

Let $a \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a > 0$ and let $r \in \mathbb{Q}$ ([[def-rationals]]).

Every rational has a representative with positive denominator
([[lem-rat-positive-denominator]]), so write $r = m/n$ with $m \in \mathbb{Z}$
and $n$ a positive integer; a positive integer is the image of a unique natural
$\ge 1$ ([[lem-nat-embeds-int]]), and we write $n$ for that natural too. Define

$$a^{r} := \big(a^{1/n}\big)^{m},$$

where $a^{1/n}$ is the unique nonnegative $n$-th root of $a$
([[thm-nth-roots-exist]]) and the outer exponent is an integer power
([[def-integer-power]]). The outer power is legitimate because $a^{1/n} > 0$ when
$a > 0$, so it has an inverse and negative integer exponents are allowed.

**Well-definedness.** The right-hand side must not depend on which representative
$m/n$ of $r$ was chosen. It does not: that is [[lem-rational-power-well-defined]],
which is recorded in this item's `justified_by` rather than in its `deps`, since
it is a statement *about* the operation defined here and therefore depends on
this definition.

**The base must be positive.** For $a < 0$ the same formula is not a definition
at all, because different representatives of the same rational give different
answers, or no answer: see [[fs-rational-power-of-negative-base]], which is
exactly the item that justifies the restriction.

**Supplementary clause for the base $0$.** For $a = 0$ and rational $r > 0$
([[def-rat-order]]) the displayed formula still makes sense and still does not
depend on the representative: $r > 0$ forces $m \ge 1$, and
$\big(0^{1/n}\big)^{m} = 0^{m} = 0$ ([[thm-nth-roots-exist]] applies to every
$a \ge 0$). So we set $0^{r} = 0$ for rational $r > 0$. For $r < 0$ the
expression $0^{r}$ is left undefined, since $0$ has no inverse. This clause is
what lets the inequalities later on this page be stated for nonnegative entries
rather than for positive ones only.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a, b > 0$ and let $r, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, with
rational powers as in [[def-rational-power]]. Then:

1. $a^{r} > 0$.
2. $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$.
3. $(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$; in particular $\big(ab\big)^{1/N} = a^{1/N} b^{1/N}$ for every natural $N \ge 1$.
4. $a^{-r} = \big(a^{r}\big)^{-1} = 1/a^{r}$.
5. $\big(a^{r}\big)^{s} = a^{rs}$.

Claims 2 and 3 persist in the supplementary case of [[def-rational-power]]: for
$a, b \ge 0$ and rationals $r, s > 0$ ([[def-rat-order]]) one still has
$(ab)^{r} = a^{r} b^{r}$ and $a^{r+s} = a^{r} a^{s}$. The two identities degenerate
differently, and it is worth saying how. In the product identity, a zero base on
either side makes both sides $0$. In the addition identity only the base $a$
occurs, so it degenerates only when $a = 0$, and then both sides are $0$; when
$a > 0$ that identity holds with no hypothesis on $b$ at all.

Let $F$ be a complete ordered field ([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Then every
$a \in F$ with $a \ge 0$ has a **unique** $s \in F$ with $s \ge 0$ and $s^2 = a$;
we write $s = \sqrt{a}$. Consequently the positive elements of $F$ are exactly the
nonzero squares: $x > 0$ if and only if $x = y^2$ for some $y \neq 0$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field. For $a, b \ge 0$:

$$a < b \iff a^2 < b^2, \qquad a \le b \iff a^2 \le b^2.$$

More generally, for arbitrary $a, b \in F$, $a^2 < b^2 \iff |a| < |b|$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) with positive cone $P$, and
let $a, b \in F$.

1. If $a > 0$ then $a^{-1} > 0$.
2. If $0 < a < b$ then $0 < b^{-1} < a^{-1}$.

An **ordered field** is a field $F$ ([[def-field]]) together with a subset
$P \subseteq F$, the set of **positive** elements (the *positive cone*),
satisfying:

- **(O1) Trichotomy.** For each $x \in F$, exactly one of the following holds:
  $x \in P$, or $x = 0$, or $-x \in P$.
- **(O2) Closure.** If $x, y \in P$ then $x + y \in P$ and $x \cdot y \in P$.

We write $x > 0$ for $x \in P$ (read "$x$ is positive"), and define the order by

$$a < b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; b - a \in P, \qquad a \le b \;:\Longleftrightarrow\; a < b \text{ or } a = b.$$

Thus $a > b$ means $b < a$, and $a \ge b$ means $b \le a$. An element $x$ with
$-x \in P$ (equivalently $x < 0$) is called **negative**.

Let $\mathbb{R}$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]), let
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $n \in \mathbb{N}$, with powers as in
[[def-integer-power]].

1. **Signs.** If $a \ge 0$ then $a^n \ge 0$, and if $a > 0$ then $a^n > 0$.
2. **Strict monotonicity in the base.** If $0 \le a < b$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n < b^n$. Consequently, for $a, b \ge 0$ and $n \ge 1$: $a < b \iff a^n < b^n$ and $a \le b \iff a^n \le b^n$, and $x \mapsto x^n$ is injective on $\{x \in \mathbb{R} : x \ge 0\}$.
3. **Comparison with the base.** If $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; if $a > 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a > 1$; and if $0 \le a \le 1$ then $a^n \le 1$.
4. **Monotonicity in the exponent.** If $a > 1$ then $a^m < a^n$ whenever $m < n$ in $\mathbb{N}$; if $a = 1$ then $a^n = 1$ for all $n$; and if $0 < a < 1$ then $a^m > a^n$ whenever $m < n$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

Let $X:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S,\Sigma)$ be a random element, let
$\mathbb P_X$ be its law, and let $g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb R$ or
$g:(S,\Sigma)\to\mathbb C$ be measurable.

1. If $g\ge0$, then
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$
2. If $g(X)$ is integrable, then $g$ is integrable with respect to
   $\mathbb P_X$ and the same formula holds:
   $$\mathbb E[g(X)]=\int_S g\,d\mathbb P_X.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

1. If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt,$$
   where the right-hand side may be $+\infty$.
2. If $X$ is an integrable real random variable, then
   $$\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X>t)\,dt-\int_0^\infty \mathbb P(X<-t)\,dt.$$

For every rational $p$,
$$\int_1^\infty x^{-p}\,dx\ \text{converges exactly when }p>1,$$
and
$$\int_0^1 x^{-p}\,dx\ \text{converges exactly when }p<1.$$
When they converge, their values are respectively $1/(p-1)$ and $1/(1-p)$.

Fix $d\ge1$ and a real function $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$. For each nonempty coordinate subset $u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}$, restrict $f$ to the face adjacent to the all-ones corner by setting
$$f_u(x_u):=f(z),\qquad z_j=\begin{cases}x_j,&j\in u,\\1,&j\notin u.\end{cases}$$
For a finite coordinate grid on $[0,1]^{|u|}$, write its cells as $R_k=\prod_{j\in u}[t_{j,k_j},t_{j,k_j+1}]$. For a cell with lower and upper vertices $a,b$, define its alternating increment
$$\Delta(f_u;R_k):=\sum_{\epsilon\in\{0,1\}^{|u|}}(-1)^{|u|-|\epsilon|}f_u(z_\epsilon),$$
where $(z_\epsilon)_j=a_j$ if $\epsilon_j=0$ and $(z_\epsilon)_j=b_j$ if $\epsilon_j=1$. The **Vitali variation** of $f_u$ is
$$V_V(f_u):=\sup_{\text{finite coordinate grids on }[0,1]^{|u|}}\ \sum_k|\Delta(f_u;R_k)|.$$
The **Hardy–Krause variation anchored at the upper corner** is
$$V_{HK,1}(f):=\sum_{\emptyset\ne u\subseteq\{1,\ldots,d\}}V_V(f_u),$$
with value $+infty$ if any summand is infinite. For $d=1$ this is the ordinary total variation on $[0,1]$. The anchor is part of the convention: every coordinate outside $u$ is fixed at $1$. The smooth mixed-derivative formula for this convention is proved separately for $C^d$ functions.

The same Vitali-variation definition applies on a nondegenerate rectangle
$R=\prod_{j=1}^q[a_j,b_j]$: each coordinate grid starts at $a_j$ and ends at
$b_j$. For a subrectangle $R\subseteq[0,1]^d$, write $V_{HK,1}(f;R)$ for the
sum of the Vitali variations of its face restrictions with complementary
coordinates fixed at the upper endpoints of $R$. If a varied side has length
zero, that face's Vitali variation is defined to be zero. For $R=[0,1]^d$ this
notation is exactly $V_{HK,1}(f)$.

Let $N\ge1$ and let $P=(x_0,\ldots,x_{N-1})$ be a finite nonempty point multiset in $[0,1)^d$. If $f:[0,1]^d\to\mathbb R$ has finite Hardy–Krause variation anchored at $1$, then
$$\left|Q_P(f)-I_d(f)\right|\le D_N^*(P)V_{HK,1}(f),$$
where $Q_P$, $I_d$, and $D_N^*$ use the conventions of [[def-star-discrepancy-and-digital-net]], and $V_{HK,1}$ uses the face convention of [[def-hardykrause-variation]]. The point set and integrand are otherwise arbitrary; no construction-specific rate or computability of the two factors is asserted.

derivations.claim: On $[0,1)$ define $g(u)=(1-u)^{-1/2}$. Since $0<1-u\le1$, [F6] gives $g(u)\ge1$. For $x<1$, the sublevel set $\{u:g(u)\le x\}$ is empty. For $x\ge1$, [F6] gives $g(u)\le x$ exactly when $x^{-2}\le1-u$, so this sublevel set is $[0,1-x^{-2}]$ (with the endpoint interpreted inside $[0,1)$). Each such set is Borel. Since the half-lines in [F3] generate the target Borel sigma-algebra and preimages commute with complements and countable unions, [F2] shows that $g$ is measurable. Thus $X:=g(U)$ is a real random variable by [F1] and [F4].

For $n\ge1$ put $u_n=1-2^{-2n}$. By [F7], $0<u_n<1$. The unique nonnegative square root of $(2^{-n})^2$ is $2^{-n}$, so [F6] gives $g(u_n)=2^n$. Given $M>0$, choose $n$ with $2^{-n}<2/(M+1)$ using [F7]; then $g(u_n)>(M+1)/2$. The grid with knots $0<u_n<1$ has variation at least $|g(u_n)-g(0)|+|g(1)-g(u_n)|=2g(u_n)-1>M$. Hence $V_{HK,1}(g)=\infty$ by [F12].

By [F5] and [A1], the distribution function of $X$ is $F_X(x)=0$ for $x<1$ and $F_X(x)=1-x^{-2}$ for $x\ge1$. For each $u<1$, $F_X(g(u))=1-(g(u))^{-2}=u$, so $g$ is the inverse-CDF transform on $[0,1)$.

For $0\le t<1$, $X\ge1$ gives $\mathbb P(X>t)=1$. For $t\ge1$, [F6] gives $X>t$ exactly when $U>1-t^{-2}$, and [A1] then gives $\mathbb P(X>t)=t^{-2}$. By [F8], [F10], and [F11] with $p=2$, $\mathbb E[X]=\int_0^1 1\,dt+\int_1^\infty t^{-2}\,dt=1+1=2$.

By [F9], change of variables for expectation applied to the measurable nonnegative $g$ and random element $U$ identifies $\mathbb E[X]$ with $\int g\,d\mathbb P_U$. By [F8] and step 2.2 this value is finite and equals $2$.

The expectation is finite by step 3.1, but the integrand has infinite upper-anchor variation by step 1.2. Therefore the finite-variation hypothesis in [F13] fails, so Koksma–Hlawka yields no finite error bound for this integrand.
